title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and an emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification), we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents with gpt-5-mini and a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed with 144 episodes (72 pairs) and 72 model calls. All baseline executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected-fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). This degenerate confirmatory outcome is internally consistent with the preregistered estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics: when identical generated candidates produce no baseline execution faults, interposing a verifier cannot reduce executed faults. We report full preregistration rationale, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, exact inferential outputs, and concrete methodological recommendations (independent-generation arms, adversarial task sets, repair-enabled pipelines) required to measure verifier utility under realistic error regimes.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for intent‑driven network configuration tasks where high‑level operator goals are translated into low‑level device commands. Prior controlled studies demonstrate promising intent→configuration accuracy in constrained vendor dialects [1], and prototype tool‑augmented stacks integrate validators to reduce regressions in NetOps workflows [2]. Nevertheless, the operational risk that a generated configuration silently violates reachability, policy, or ordering invariants remains a key barrier to adoption. A standard mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that deterministically checks generated candidates before execution and optionally triggers repairs or human review [3].

This paper reports a preregistered, deterministic paired experiment that asks a narrow, operationally meaningful question: when the identical LLM candidate is evaluated both without and with a canonical deterministic verifier (shared_initial_candidate semantics), does the verifier reduce the proportion of candidates that would execute with operational faults in an isolated emulation environment? We selected this estimand to measure pure verifier detection performance on identical generator outputs, avoiding confounding by generator sampling variation.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) that couples a modern LLM (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini) with a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and an isolated emulator. (2) Deterministic execution accounting and archived traces showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (no baseline faults) with exact inferential outputs and bootstrap details. (3) Concrete methodological analysis explaining why the design produced a ceiling effect and specifying alternative experimental contracts required to evaluate verifier utility under realistic error regimes (independent generation, repair‑enabled flow, adversarial tasks).
sections.related_work:
LLM‑based intent→configuration translation has been demonstrated in controlled evaluations where in‑context learning or task‑specific tuning produces high task accuracy over limited dialects [1]. Work on tool‑augmented multi‑agent frameworks and NetOps co‑pilots illustrates architectures that include verification components to reduce regressions, but public evaluations that preregister verifier detection performance against executed outcomes are sparse [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed and instantiated across software engineering domains to combine stochastic generation with deterministic checks and iterative repair; these works motivate applying GVR to NetOps but do not provide a canonical, artifact‑grounded end‑to‑end evaluation pairing LLM generators with network verifiers and emulated execution traces [3].

Classical deterministic network verification techniques (e.g., header‑space analysis and policy checkers) provide efficient reachability and policy invariants that are natural verifier candidates in NetOps GVR stacks [4]. Our work situates a preregistered, paired experimental test within this literature: we do not attempt to evaluate every GVR variant, nor to claim production readiness; instead, we measure the specific paired estimand—verifier detection capability on identical generated candidates—under reproducible, archived conditions and identify the limits of conclusions that such a design supports.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 before observing outcomes and froze design, sampling, and analysis code. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The confirmatory hypothesis H1 prespecified a paired two‑sided test targeting an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 with alpha = 0.05 and power ≥ 0.80; the registered sample size was N = 72 pairs stratified across three topology complexity strata (small/medium/complex).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and design rationale. Per the execution_contract, each intent received exactly one initial LLM generation (shared across conditions). Under baseline the identical candidate is executed in the emulator and the outcome recorded; under guarded the deterministic verifier is run on the same candidate and, if it flags violations, the outcome is recorded as "prevented" (no emulator execution); if the verifier does not flag, the candidate is executed. This contract isolates verifier detection on identical outputs rather than conflating verifier benefits arising from repaired or alternate candidates.

Model, adapter, and verifier details. The recorded model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json) declares requested_model = gpt-5-mini, provider = openai_responses, and shows temperature = null (provider default sampling semantics applied at runtime). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0"); scoring used rule full_intent_constraint_validation and produced binary per‑episode scores plus detailed validator_trace fields (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before, validation_after and normalized_configuration). The recorded model_configuration.json and verifier traces are authoritative artifacts in the evidence bundle.

Task bank generation, constraints, and contamination checks. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each manifest entry contains: explicit intent, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, difficulty metadata, initial and expected final state, and a source_identifier (synthetic‑netops:task‑...). Per preregistration, exact‑match contamination checks against public corpora were applied and would cause exclusion; in the executed run no confirmatory pairs were excluded. The task bank intentionally included workflow policies (e.g., make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore) to probe sequencing and dependency constraints.

Execution protocol, retries, and missingness. The missingness_plan allowed up to two transient retries for hosted‑API errors. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 144 (72 pairs × 2 conditions), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 72 (one shared generation per pair). Provider call accounting and stage counts (shared_initial_generation = 72, cache_miss_count = 72) are archived in deterministic_reconciliation.json. Any technical retries, timestamps, and failure reasons would be logged per the preregistered manifest; none occurred for confirmatory pairs.

Scoring and statistical analysis. The validator produced episode‑level binary outcomes (valid configuration vs. violation) and detailed traces. The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute the paired contingency table and run an exact McNemar two‑sided test where applicable. We computed paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the paired difference and descriptive rates with 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729 (recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Pre‑specified subgroup confirmatory comparisons (topology complexity and policy type) were planned with Holm correction; these remain exploratory when baseline variation is absent.

Reproducible artifact pointers. The authoritative artifacts for reproduction include: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. The analysis bootstrap seed (1729) and resamples (10000) are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl; the paired analysis executor and inputs are archived and deterministic.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and consistency. The run completed without technical failures. Key deterministic artifact counts: planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72. Provider call audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 72 and completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 72. These counts are reconciled in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and provider_call_audit fields.

Paired contingency and inferential outputs. Aggregating across 72 pairs yields contingency counts n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. The paired estimate paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. The per‑condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline success_rate = 1.0 and guarded success_rate = 1.0. These numeric outputs and the analysis scripts are archived as analysis/* artifacts.

Representative validator traces and diagnostics. Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json) show that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parsed and validated required command sequences for each shared candidate. Example archived trace fields present for each episode include: parsed_command_count (2–6 depending on task), required_command_count, difficulty.level (medium/hard/very_hard), normalized_configuration, validation_before and validation_after states, validator_version = "5.0", and score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION" for the sampled examples. These traces confirm the verifier ran and found no violations on the generated candidates in this task bank.

Contamination, exclusions, and missingness summary. Per the execution manifest and analysis/contamination_summary.csv, no confirmatory pairs were excluded for exact‑match contamination. The missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 72 and zero failed or unscorable episodes across conditions. The absence of exclusions and failures simplifies interpretation but also contributes to the degenerate inferential result.

Sensitivity and secondary checks. Planned sensitivity analyses (e.g., treating excluded pairs as failures, bootstrap checks) were executable on the archived artifacts. Because there were no excluded pairs and no discordant outcomes, these sensitivity analyses produce the same degenerate numerical conclusion. The analysis log records the deterministic bootstrap seed and resample count, allowing exact reproduction of the CI collapse to a point mass at 0.0.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory interpretation: ceiling/null outcome. The preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics validly isolates verifier detection performance on identical generated candidates. Observing zero baseline faults yields a scientifically informative null/ceiling outcome: under the tested model, prompt/template, and task bank the generator outputs were uniformly valid in the emulator and the verifier had no faults to prevent. The numeric outputs (n_11 = 72, p = 1.0, bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0]) accurately reflect this state and are precisely reproducible from the archived artifacts.

Why the ceiling effect matters for experimental design. The shared_initial_candidate contract intentionally avoids conflating differences arising from stochastic sampling or repair‑enabled iterations. That choice trades sensitivity to verifier utility mediated via repairs for strict measurement of detection on identical outputs. When baseline error prevalence is low, a design that permits independent generation per condition, multiple samples, or adversarially crafted tasks is required to produce non‑degenerate paired comparisons and to measure verifier tradeoffs (true positives vs false positives) under realistic error regimes.

Design recommendations for measuring verifier utility. (1) Independent‑generation arms: permit separate generator calls per condition to capture how verifier‑triggered repairs or alternate candidates affect executed outcomes. (2) Repair‑enabled flow: allow a single deterministic repair call when the verifier flags a candidate and measure repaired candidate execution outcomes to quantify end‑to‑end benefit. (3) Adversarial and fault‑injection tasks: enrich the task bank with intentionally difficult sequencing and semantic perturbations to increase baseline error prevalence and reveal verifier detection sensitivity. (4) Multi‑model and sampling parameter sweeps: compare across models and explicit sampling parameters (avoid temperature=null) to quantify robustness and sampling‑sensitivity.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: adopting one shared generation per intent and leaving temperature = null in the archived model_configuration.json means provider default sampling governed generation; this residual sampling uncertainty is recorded in the artifacts. Construct validity: emulator‑observed faults are a conservative proxy for operational harm but may not capture traffic‑dependent, time‑varying, or cross‑device emergent failures present in production. External validity: results are specific to gpt-5-mini, the synthetic/emulated task bank, and the deterministic verifier used; extrapolation to other models, vendor dialects, or production devices is not supported. Conclusion validity: with zero baseline failures the confirmatory design has no power to detect verifier benefit; the preregistered power analysis assumed a nonzero baseline error rate.

Operational implications and responsible interpretation. The absence of baseline faults here suggests that, under constrained prompts, dialects, and emulator settings, modern LLMs can produce high task accuracy. This should not be interpreted as production safety. Instead, organizations should treat verifiers as part of layered defenses whose utility depends on realistic error prevalence; the experimental path to demonstrating operational benefit requires task realism, adversarial stress tests, and repair‑orchestration arms.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). The evidence‑grounded conclusion is conditional: verifier benefit depends on generator error prevalence and task realism. Future confirmatory measurements of verifier utility should use experimental contracts that permit independent/multiple generations, repair‑enabled flows, adversarial task banks, and multi‑model comparisons. All execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis logs referenced in this manuscript are archived in the evidence bundle to support replication and follow‑on studies.

limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is a residual uncertainty recorded in the archived configuration.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
